prompt: True or False: It is mandatory that the product Increment be released to production at the end of each Sprint.

options.text: True
False

note: A usable Increment may be released before the Sprint ends; Scrum does not require a release at every Sprint boundary.

prompt: When should a Developer on a Scrum Team be replaced?

options.text: Never, it reduces productivity.
Every Sprint to promote shared learning.
As needed, while taking into account a short-term reduction in productivity.
As needed, with no special allowance for changes in productivity.

note: Scrum does not prescribe when to replace a Developer, but team changes can temporarily reduce productivity as people adapt.

prompt: Which statement best describes the Sprint Review?

options.text: It is a mechanism to control Developer activity during a Sprint.
It is when the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of a Sprint and figure out what to do next.
It is a demo at the end of the Sprint for everyone in the organization to check on the work done.

note: The Sprint Review is a working session to inspect the outcome with stakeholders and adapt what to do next, not merely a demo.

prompt: Who is on the Scrum Team?

options.text: Project Manager.
Developers.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.

note: The Scrum Team consists of one Product Owner, one Scrum Master, and Developers; “project manager” is not a Scrum accountability.

prompt: The CEO asks the Developers to add a "very important" item to a Sprint that is in progress. What should the Developers do?

options.text: Add the item to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
Add the item to the current Sprint Backlog and do whatever amount of work is necessary to meet the Sprint Goal while satisfying the CEO.
Discuss the item with the other members of the Scrum Team so the team can decide what to do.
Add the item to the current Sprint Backlog, drop an item of similar size, and reduce the Sprint Goal.

note: The Developers and Product Owner can discuss scope changes during the Sprint, but no stakeholder can unilaterally add work or change the Sprint Goal.

prompt: Who is required to attend the Daily Scrum?

options.text: The Developers and Product Owner.
The Scrum Master and Product Owner.
The Scrum Team.
The Developers and Scrum Master.
The Developers.

note: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers; the Product Owner or Scrum Master joins in that capacity only when actively working on Sprint Backlog items.

prompt: What is the function or purpose of Management in Scrum?

options.text: Support the Product Owner with insights and information into high value product and system capabilities. Support the Scrum Master to encourage organizational change that fosters empiricism, self-management, bottom-up intelligence, and intelligent product delivery.
Continually monitor staffing levels of the Scrum Team.
Identify and remove people that are not working hard enough.
Monitor the progress of the Developers on the Scrum Team.

note: Management supports the Product Owner with product insight and helps the Scrum Master foster an environment for Scrum; it does not direct Developers’ daily work.
caveat: Source caveat: management is not a formal Scrum accountability. This question describes supportive practices; scoring follows the supplied bank.

prompt: Which of the following services is appropriate for a Scrum Master in regard to the Daily Scrum?

options.text: Lead the discussions of the Developers.
Ensure that all 3 questions have been answered.
Facilitate in a way that ensures each team member has a chance to speak.
Teach the Developers to keep the Daily Scrum within the 15 minute timebox.
All answers apply.

note: The Scrum Master ensures the Daily Scrum takes place and may teach its 15-minute timebox, but Developers choose its format rather than answering prescribed questions.

prompt: The three pillars of Scrum are:

options.text: Respect For People, Kaizen, Eliminating Waste.
Planning, Inspection, Adaptation.
Planning, Demonstration, Retrospective.
Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation.
Transparency, Eliminating Waste, Kaizen.

note: Transparency makes work inspectable, and inspection informs adaptation—the three pillars underlying Scrum.

prompt: The Developers should have all the skills needed to:

options.text: Turn the Product Backlog items they select into an Increment of a useful and valuable product.
Complete the project as estimated when the date and cost are committed to the Product Owner.
Do all of the development work, except for specialized testing that requires additional tools and environments.

note: Cross-functionality means the Developers collectively have the skills needed to create a valuable, useful Increment, including testing.

prompt: What does it mean to say that an event has a timebox?

options.text: The event can take no more than a maximum amount of time.
The event must happen at a set time.
The event must take at least a minimum amount of time.
The event must happen by a given time.

note: A timebox sets the event’s maximum duration; it does not require the event to last that long or start at a particular time.

prompt: Who creates the Definition of Done?

options.text: The Product Owner since they are responsible for the product's success.
The Scrum Master since they are responsible for the productivity of the Developers.
If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
The Scrum Team, in a collaborative effort where the result is the common denominator of all members' definitions.

note: The Scrum Team follows an organizational Definition of Done when one exists; otherwise, it creates one appropriate for the product.

prompt: The timebox for the Sprint Review is:

options.text: As long as needed.
2 hours.
4 hours for a monthly Sprint. For shorter Sprints it is usually shorter.
4 hours and longer as needed.
1 day.

note: The Guide sets a four-hour maximum for a one-month Sprint Review and says it is usually shorter for shorter Sprints.

prompt: When many Scrum Teams are working on a single product, what best describes the Definition of Done?

options.text: Each Scrum Team uses its own, but must make their definition clear to all other teams so the differences are known.
It depends.
All Scrum Teams must have a Definition of Done that makes their combined Increment valuable and useful.

note: Teams working on one product must share a Definition of Done so their combined Increment is coherent and usable.

prompt: Who is responsible for managing the progress of work during a Sprint?

options.text: The Product Owner.
The most junior member of the team.
The Developers.
The Scrum Master.

note: Developers manage their work and progress toward the Sprint Goal; the Scrum Master does not manage their tasks.

prompt: When does a Developer become accountable for the value of a Product Backlog item selected for the Sprint?

options.text: Whenever a team member can accommodate more work.
At the Sprint Planning Event.
During the Daily Scrum.
Never. The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating value every Sprint.

note: The Scrum Team is collectively accountable for creating a valuable Increment; value is not assigned to one Developer per item.

prompt: What are two ways a Scrum Master serves to enable effective Scrum Teams?

options.text: By starting and ending the meetings at the proper time.
By facilitating Developer decision-making.
By keeping high value features high in the Product Backlog.
By removing impediments that hinder the Scrum Team.

note: The Scrum Master enables self-management by facilitating decision-making and helping remove impediments, rather than directing the Developers.

prompt: When does a Sprint conclude?

options.text: When the Sprint Retrospective is complete.
When all the tasks are completed by the Developers.
When the Product Owner decides enough has been delivered to meet the Sprint Goal.
When all Product Backlog items meet their Definition of Done.

note: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint; unfinished work does not extend its fixed timebox.

prompt: The length of a Sprint should be:

options.text: Short enough to keep the business risk acceptable to the Product Owner.
Short enough to be able to synchronize the development work with other business events.
One month or less.
All of the above.

note: Sprints are one month or less; shorter cycles can limit risk and create more frequent opportunities for feedback and learning.

prompt:
The Developers should not be interrupted during the Sprint and the Sprint Goal should remain intact. These are conditions that foster creativity, quality and productivity.

(Which one of the following answers is FALSE?)

options.text: As a decomposition of the selected Product Backlog items, the Sprint Backlog changes and may grow as the work emerges.
The Product Owner can help clarify or optimize the Sprint when asked by the Developers.
The Developers may work with the Product Owner to add or remove work if they find themselves with more or less capacity than expected.
The Sprint Backlog is fully formulated in the Sprint Planning event and does not change during the Sprint.

note: The Sprint Backlog is updated as work emerges, and scope can be renegotiated with the Product Owner while the Sprint Goal remains intact.

prompt: The timebox for the Sprint Planning event is?

options.text: Monthly.
Whenever it is done.
8 hours for a monthly Sprint. For shorter Sprints it is usually shorter.
4 hours.

note: Sprint Planning is at most eight hours for a one-month Sprint; shorter Sprints usually have shorter planning events.

prompt: What is the typical size for a Scrum Team?

options.text: Minimum of 7.
7 plus or minus 2.
10 or fewer.

note: The 2020 Guide says Scrum Teams are typically 10 or fewer people; this is guidance, not a rigid Scrum limit.

prompt: How much work must the Developers complete for each Sprint?

options.text: All development work and at least some testing.
Enough so that the Increment meets the Definition of Done.
As much as it can fit into the Sprint.
Analysis, design, programming, testing and documentation.

note: Only work meeting the Definition of Done is part of the Increment; partial testing or unfinished work does not qualify.

prompt: An organization has decided to adopt Scrum, but management wants to change the terminology to fit with terminology already used. What will likely happen if this is done?

options.text: Without a new vocabulary as a reminder of the change, very little change may actually happen.
The organization may not understand what has changed with Scrum and the benefits of Scrum may be lost.
Management may feel less anxious.
All of the above.

note: The key treats all listed effects as likely, but the Guide warns against changing Scrum’s core elements; renaming terms alone cannot predict these outcomes.

prompt: When does a Developer become the sole owner of an item on the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: Never. All items in the Sprint Backlog are "owned" by the Developers on the Scrum Team.
At the Sprint Planning event.
Whenever a team member can accommodate more work.
During the Daily Scrum.

note: The Developers collectively own and manage the Sprint Backlog; Scrum does not assign each item to a sole owner.

prompt: When does the next Sprint begin?

options.text: When the Product Owner is ready.
Immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
Next Monday.
Immediately following the next Sprint Planning.

note: A new Sprint begins immediately after the previous Sprint concludes, with no prescribed gap between them.

prompt: What are three incorrect, untrue, or misleading statements about Scrum?

options.text: Scrum is a framework for developing and sustaining complex products.
Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking.
Scrum is like traditional processes but with self-organization to replace Project Managers.
Scrum is a framework that eliminates complexity.
Each component of Scrum serves a specific purpose and is essential to your ability to use Scrum to develop complex products.
Scrum is a methodology where you can pick and choose which parts of Scrum you think will work for your environment.

note: Scrum is a framework for complex work, not a replacement hierarchy or a method for eliminating complexity or selectively omitting framework elements.

prompt: When might a Sprint be cancelled?

options.text: When the Developers feel that the work is too hard.
When it becomes clear that not everything will be finished by the end of the Sprint.
When the sales department has an important new opportunity.
When the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

note: Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and only when its Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

prompt: True or False: The Scrum Team must choose at least one high priority process improvement item, identified during the Sprint Retrospective, and place it in the Sprint Backlog.

options.text: True
False

note: The Scrum Team should address its most impactful improvement as soon as possible, but Scrum does not require adding one to every Sprint Backlog.

prompt: Why is the Daily Scrum held at the same time and same place?

options.text: The Product Owner demands it.
The place can be named.
The consistency reduces complexity.
Rooms are hard to book and this lets it be booked in advance.

note: The Guide calls for the Daily Scrum at the same time and place every working day to reduce complexity.

prompt: What is the main reason for the Scrum Master to be at the Daily Scrum?
context: [Related to Question 6 and Question 8 - but tests a different aspect: the Scrum Master's main reason for being at the Daily Scrum]

options.text: To gather status and progress information to report to management.
They do not have to be there; they only need to ensure the Developers have a Daily Scrum.
To write down any changes to the Sprint Backlog, including adding new items, and tracking progress on the burn-down.
To make sure every team member answers the three questions.

note: The Scrum Master need not attend the Daily Scrum, but is accountable for ensuring that it takes place.

prompt: During a Sprint, a Developer determines that the Scrum Team will not be able to complete the items in their forecast. Who should be present to review and adjust the Product Backlog items selected?
context: [Related to Question 5 and Question 20 - but tests a different aspect: who is present to renegotiate Sprint scope when the forecast cannot be completed]

options.text: The Product Owner and the Developers.
The Developers.
The Product Owner and all stakeholders.
The Scrum Master, the project manager, and the Developers

note: Developers and the Product Owner can renegotiate selected work as new information emerges, while keeping the Sprint Goal intact.
caveat: Source caveat: this canonical entry has a complete prompt and a related-question annotation, both preserved here. Interpret scope adjustment in the context of the Sprint Goal; scoring follows the supplied bank.

prompt: Which Scrum events are timeboxed?
context: [Related to Question 11, Question 13 and Question 21 - but tests a different aspect: identifying which events are timeboxed]

options.text: Release Retrospective.
Sprint Planning.
Sprint Testing.
Refinement.
Sprint Retrospective.
Sprint Review.
Release Testing.

note: These listed Scrum events are timeboxed; the Daily Scrum is also timeboxed to 15 minutes but is not among the choices.

prompt: True or False: When multiple Scrum Teams work together on the same product, each team should maintain a separate Product Backlog.
context: [Related to Question 14 - but tests a different aspect: Product Backlog (not Definition of Done) with multiple teams]

options.text: True
False

note: A product has one Product Backlog, ordered by its Product Owner, even when several Scrum Teams contribute to it.

prompt: True or False: The purpose of a Sprint is to produce a valuable and useful Increment of a usable product.
context: [Related to Question 18 and Question 28 - but tests a different aspect: the purpose of a Sprint]

options.text: True
False

note: Each Sprint aims to produce a valuable, useful Increment; it is not a phase for completing plans before delivering value.

prompt: The Product Backlog is ordered by:

options.text: Items are randomly arranged.
Whatever is deemed most appropriate by the Product Owner.
Risk, where safer items are at the top, and riskier items are at the bottom.
Least valuable items at the top to most valuable at the bottom.
Size, where small items are at the top and large items are at the bottom.

note: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog to best support value, considering factors such as risk, dependencies, and learning.

prompt: True or False: Scrum has a role called "project manager."
context: [Related to Question 4 and Question 27 - but tests a different aspect: whether a project manager role exists in Scrum]

options.text: True
False

note: Scrum defines the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers accountabilities, but no project-manager role.

prompt: Which statement best describes Scrum?
context: [Related to Question 27 - but tests a different aspect: how Scrum is defined as a framework]

options.text: A defined and predictive process that conforms to the principles of Scientific Management.
A cookbook that defines best practices for software development.
A framework for creating complex products in complex environments.
A complete methodology that defines how to develop software.

note: Scrum is a framework for creating complex products in complex environments, not a complete software-development methodology.

prompt: Which statement best describes a Product Owner's responsibility?
context: [Related to Question 7 and Question 17 - but tests a different aspect: Product Owner responsibility]

options.text: Managing the project and ensuring that the work meets the commitments to the stakeholders.
Keep stakeholders from distracting the Developers.
Maximizing the value of the work the Scrum Team does.
Directing the Developers.

note: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team’s work.

prompt: Who has the final say on the order of the Product Backlog?
context: [Related to Question 36 and Question 39 - but tests a different aspect: who has the final say on Product Backlog order]

options.text: The Product Owner.
The CEO.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
The Stakeholders.

note: The Product Owner is accountable for Product Backlog ordering; others may advise but do not have final authority over it.

prompt: Which of the following are examples of a Scrum Team practicing Scrum poorly or not exhibiting traits of a self-managing Scrum Team?
context: [Related to Question 6 and Question 15 - but tests a different aspect: recognizing poor Scrum practice / lack of self-management]

options.text: Stakeholders attend the Daily Scrum to check on the Scrum Team's progress.
The Developers invite external stakeholders to the Sprint Planning to ask them how to turn a Product Backlog item into an Increment via a complete and detailed Sprint Backlog.
The Developers are collaboratively selecting their own work during the Sprint.
The Developers have all the skills they need to create a valuable, useful Increment.
The Developers are working within the boundaries of their organization's functional description and nicely handing off work from analyst to developer to tester to integration.
The Developers create their own Sprint Backlog, reflecting all work that is required to meet the Definition of Done.

note: Daily Scrum status-checking and functional handoffs conflict with Developer self-management; planning invitees may advise, so option B’s directive framing matters.

prompt: Who should know the most about the progress toward a business objective or a release, and be able to explain the alternatives most clearly?
context: [Related to Question 39 and Question 40 - but tests a different aspect: who knows most about progress toward a business objective or release]

options.text: The Product Owner
The Project Manager
The Developers
The Scrum Master

note: The Product Owner manages the Product Backlog and works with stakeholders, making them best placed to explain progress and product options.

prompt: What should the Scrum Team do during the first Sprint?
context: [Related to Question 35 - but tests a different aspect: what the Scrum Team does during the first Sprint]

options.text: Create a valuable and useful Increment.
Create the complete Product Backlog to be developed in subsequent Sprints.
Determine the complete architecture and infrastructure for the product.
Develop a plan for the rest of the release.

note: The first Sprint should produce a valuable, useful Increment; Scrum does not require completing architecture or the entire backlog first.

prompt: The timebox for a Daily Scrum is?
context: [Related to Question 8, Question 11 and Question 33 - but tests a different aspect: the specific timebox of the Daily Scrum]

options.text: 4 hours.
The same time of day every day.
Two minutes per person.
15 minutes for a 4-week sprint. For shorter Sprints it is usually shorter.
15 minutes.

note: The Daily Scrum has a fixed 15-minute timebox, regardless of Sprint length.

prompt: What factor should be considered when establishing the Sprint length ?

options.text: The need for the team to learn based on doing work and measuring results.
The organization's release schedule.
The frequency at which team formation can be changed.
The organization has mandated similar length sprints.

note: Frequent learning and feedback can inform Sprint length, but Scrum prescribes only a fixed Sprint of one month or less—not this single selection factor.

prompt: Which two ways of creating Scrum Teams are consistent with Scrum's values?

options.text: Existing teams propose how they would like to go about organizing into the new structure
Managers personally re-assign current subordinates to new teams.
Managers collaborate to assign individuals to specific teams.
Bring all the people together and let them organize into Scrum Teams
The Chief Product Owner determines the new team structures and assignments.

note: Letting people organize into teams supports self-management; Scrum does not prescribe a particular team-formation procedure.

prompt: Which of the following is an example of an Increment?

options.text: A plan for the overall product release
A mock-up of the product marketing materials
A design for the product
A product roll-out plan.
A valuable, useful set of product features.
All of the above.

note: An Increment is a usable, valuable step toward the Product Goal; plans and designs alone are not necessarily usable product outcomes.

prompt: Which outcome is expected as a Scrum Team matures?

options.text: There will be no need for a timeboxed Sprint.
They will improve their Definition of Done to include more stringent criteria.
The Sprint Retrospectives will grow to be longer than 4 hours.
A Scrum Master is no longer needed since they are a mature team now.
Sprint Reviews will no longer be needed.

note: A Scrum Team may strengthen its Definition of Done as quality improves, but the Guide does not promise this as an automatic maturity outcome.

prompt: Which technique is the best way the Scrum Master can ensure that the Developers communicate effectively with the Product Owner?

options.text: Observe communications between them and facilitate direct collaboration.
Teach the Product Owner about the technologies employed during the Sprints.
Function as a go-between for them.
Teach the Developers to talk in terms of business needs and objectives

note: The Scrum Master can support direct collaboration between Developers and the Product Owner rather than acting as their go-between.

prompt: Who is responsible for collaboration with stakeholders?

options.text: The Business Analyst.
The Scrum Team.
The Team Manager.
The Project Manager
The Developers

note: The Scrum Team collaborates with stakeholders; the Product Owner remains accountable for maximizing product value and managing stakeholder input.

prompt: How much of the Sprint Backlog must be defined during the Sprint Planning event?

options.text: Enough so the Developers can create their forecast of what work they can do
Just enough tasks for the Scrum Master to be confident in the Developers understanding of the Sprint
The entire Sprint Backlog must be identified and estimated by the end of Sprint Planning
Just enough to understand design and architectural implications.

note: Sprint Planning needs enough detail for Developers to forecast work toward the Sprint Goal; the Sprint Backlog can be elaborated during the Sprint.

prompt: One of the Scrum events is the Daily Scrum. What are two intended outcomes of the Daily Scrum?

options.text: An updated Scrum board to make Sprint progress transparent for the stakeholders.
Identification of impediments that may prevent the Developers from achieving the Sprint Goal
A status report for the upper management indicating what each individual has done, will be doing, and what is impeding him/her
A shared understanding of the most important work to be undertaken next to achieve the best possible progress toward the Sprint goal.
An update of completed tasks and of the remaining work so the Scrum Master can plan the next day.

note: Developers use the Daily Scrum to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan, not to report status to management.

prompt: A Scrum Master is introducing Scrum to a new Team. The Team has decided that a Sprint Retrospective is unnecessary, What action should the Scrum Master take?

options.text: Comply with the decision of the self-managing team
Begin facilitating productive and useful Sprint Retrospectives.
Call a meeting between the Scrum Team and senior management
Consult with the Product Owner to see how they feel about the situation

note: Sprint Retrospectives are part of Scrum, and the Scrum Master helps ensure they are productive; the Developers choose how to conduct them.

prompt: When multiple Scrum Teams are working on the same product, should all of their Increments be Integrated every Sprint?

options.text: Yes, but only for Scrum Teams whose work has dependencies.
No, that is far too hard and must be done in a hardening Sprint
No, each Scrum Team stands alone.
Yes, in order to accurately inspect what is done.

note: A usable, inspectable Increment includes integrated work; teams cannot defer integration until a later “hardening Sprint.”

prompt: Which Scrum Value is affected by a lack of trust in the Scrum Team?

options.text: Focus
Respect
Openness
Courage
Commitment
All of the above.

note: Scrum’s five values reinforce one another, so lack of trust can undermine all of them; this is an interpretation, not a separate Guide rule.

prompt: Who starts the Daily Scrum?

options.text: The Scrum Master. This ensures that the Developers have the event, and it stays within the timebox
Whoever the Developers decide should start
The customers who attend each day
The Product Owner
The person coming in last. This encourages people to be on time and helps to stay within the timebox.

note: Developers decide how to conduct their Daily Scrum; Scrum prescribes its purpose and timebox, not who speaks first.

prompt: True or False: Multiple Scrum Teams working on the same product must have the same Sprint start date

options.text: True
False.

note: The Guide does not require multiple teams to share Sprint start dates, though coordination may be useful when creating one product Increment.

prompt: You are the Scrum Master of a new, to be developed Product. Development is going to require 45 people. What is a good first question for you to suggest the group thinks about when forming into teams?

options.text: Who are the subject matter experts on each team?
How will we make sure all teams have the right amount of expertise?
Who are going to be the team leads?
What is the right mixture of senior and junior people on each team?

note: Teams need the combined skills to create a usable Increment; Scrum provides no fixed recipe for distributing expertise among 45 people.

prompt: At the end of a Sprint, a Product Backlog item worked on during the Sprint does not meet the Definition of Done What two things should happen with the undone Product Blacklog item?

options.text: Do not include the item in the increment this sprint
Put it on the Product Backlog for the Product Owner to decide what to do with it
Review the item, add the done part of the estimate to the velocity and create a Story for the remaining work
If the stakeholders agree, the Product Owner can accept it and release it to the users

note: Work that misses the Definition of Done is excluded from the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

prompt: As the Sprint Planning progresses, the Developers realize that the workload may be greater than their capacity to complete the work. Which two are valid actions?

options.text: Recruit additional Developers before the work can begin
The Developers ensure that the Scrum Team is aware, start the Sprint, and monitor progress.
The Developers work overtime during this Sprint.
Cancel the Sprint.
Remove or change selected Product Backlog items

note: Developers make their forecast transparent and can adjust selected work with the Product Owner; a capacity concern alone does not cancel the Sprint.

prompt: How do you know that a Scrum Team is cross-functional?

options.text: There are no conflicts within the Scrum Team
A few of the Developers pair program and do Test-Driven Development
The Scrum Team has all the skills to create an increment by the end of every Sprint
Every member of the Scrum Team is able to perform every task

note: Cross-functional means the Scrum Team collectively has the skills needed to create a usable Increment; it does not mean every member can do every task.

prompt: Developers are self-managing, which of the following do they manage?

options.text: Sprint length.
When to release, based on its progress.
Product Backlog ordering.
Stakeholders for the Sprint Review.
Sprint Backlog

note: Developers self-manage the Sprint Backlog, including adapting their plan as they learn more about the work.

prompt: What are two effective ways for the Scrum Team to make non-functional requirements visible?

options.text: Put them on a separate list on the Scrum board, available for all to see.
Run the integration and regression tests before the end of the Sprint, and capture the open work for the Sprint Backlog of the next Sprint.
Add them to the Product Backlog to ensure transparency
Add them to the Definition of Done so the work is taken care of every Sprint

note: Product Backlog items can describe product-specific quality needs, while the Definition of Done makes shared quality criteria transparent.

prompt: Which topics should be discussed in the Sprint Review?

options.text: The Scrum process, and how it was used during the Sprint
Coding and engineering practices.
The product Increment
All of the above

note: The Sprint Review centers on the Increment and product adaptation; inspecting the Scrum process or engineering practices belongs elsewhere.

prompt: Which Scrum Values are violated by building Product Backlog items that have low business value?

options.text: Focus
Earned Value
Respect
Economic Value Added.
Courage

note: The key maps low-value work to focus, respect, and courage, but the Guide does not prescribe a one-to-one list of values violated by this situation.

prompt: Who is responsible for the sizing of Product Backlog items?

options.text: The Scrum Master
The most senior people in the organization, including architects and subject matter experts.
The Developers after clarifying requirements with the Product Owner
The Developers, alone.
The Product Owner with input from the Developers

note: Developers are responsible for sizing Product Backlog items; the Product Owner clarifies them and may influence sizing by explaining trade-offs.

prompt: What may be included in the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: User Stories.
Tasks.
Use Cases.
Tests.
Any of the above (or others) which are a decomposition of the selected Product Backlog items.

note: Scrum does not prescribe Sprint Backlog formats; any representation may be used if it helps plan work toward the Sprint Goal.

prompt: When is it most appropriate for a Scrum Team to change the Definition of Done?

options.text: During Sprint Planning
During the Sprint Retrospective.
During Product Backlog refinement.
Prior to starting a new project.

note: The Retrospective is a natural opportunity to inspect and improve how the team works, but the Guide does not reserve Definition of Done changes to one event.

prompt: Several Sprints into a project, the Product Owner tells the Scrum Master that a key stakeholder just started using the product. The stakeholder is unhappy with the quality of the product, and the Product Owner agrees with the stakeholder's assessment that the quality is low. How should the Scrum Master respond to the Product Owner?

options.text: Tell the Product Owner they have noted the concern and will raise this issue at the Sprint Retrospective.
Work with the Product Owner to understand their desired resolution and help formulate an approach for raising the concern with the Developers.
Bring the concern to the testers to improve how the Product is verified
Encourage the Product Owner to include quality specifications in the Product Backlog and to communicate the stakeholders' concerns to the Developers
Explain to the Product Owner that it is up to the Developers to decide on acceptable quality standards.

note: Discussing the concern with the Product Owner and Developers makes quality expectations visible; quality remains a Scrum Team responsibility, not just testing’s.

prompt: A Product Owner wants advice from the Scrum Master about estimating work in Scrum. What guidance should a Scrum Master give?

options.text: Product Backlog items must be estimated in story points.
Estimates are made by the Product Owner, but are best checked with the Developers.
Estimates must be in relative units
Estimates are made by the people doing the work.
Scrum forbids estimating.

note: The people doing the work estimate it; Scrum does not require story points, relative units, or any particular estimation method.

prompt: What happens if the Scrum Team cannot complete its work by the end of the Sprint?

options.text: The Sprint is extended temporarily. Lessons are taken to ensure it does not happen again
The Sprint is extended and future Sprints use this new duration.
The Sprint length is unchanged and the Scrum Team continuously learns and adapts.

note: Sprint length stays fixed; the Scrum Team inspects what prevented completion and adapts instead of extending the Sprint.

prompt: What is the key concern when multiple Scrum Teams are working from the same Product Backlog?

options.text: Meeting original scope projections.
Clear definition of requirements.
Maximizing velocity.
Making sure there is enough work for everyone on each team

options.text: When the Scrum Master asks the Product Owner to attend.
When the Product Owner is actively working on items on the Sprint Backlog; however, they participate as a Developer.
When the Product Owner needs to represent the stakeholders' point of view to the Developers.
When there are impediments to discuss.

note: Daily Scrum explicitly states that Product Owners actively working on Sprint Backlog items participate as Developers.

prompt: Who is accountable for tracking the remaining work toward the Sprint Goal?
context: [Related to Question 15 - closely related progress-accountability question with different answer choices]

options.text: The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
The Project Manager.

note: Developers adapt their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal; Daily Scrum and Sprint Backlog make progress inspectable.

prompt: A Scrum Team is required to deliver a done Increment by the end of a Sprint. Select two statements that explain what done means.

options.text: All work the Developers are willing to do.
Ready to be released to end users.
No work is left to meet the Definition of Done.
Whatever the Product Owner defines as quality.
Ready for integration.

note: Increment and Definition of Done require usable, integrated work meeting the product's quality measures. Release readiness does not require actual release at the Sprint boundary.

prompt: What activities would a Product Owner typically undertake in the period between the end of the current Sprint and the start of the next Sprint?

options.text: There are no such activities. The next Sprint starts immediately after the current Sprint.
Refine the Product Backlog.
Work with the Quality Assurance departments on the Increment of the current Sprint.
Update the project plan with stakeholders.

note: The Sprint specifies that a new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one concludes. Refinement occurs as needed within Sprints, not in a separate gap.

prompt: The Product Owner is not collaborating with the Developers during the Sprint. What are two valuable actions for a Scrum Master to take?

options.text: Bring up the problem in the Sprint Retrospective.
Nominate a proxy Product Owner.
Stop the Sprint, send the Product Owner to a course and restart.
Coach the Product Owner in the values of Scrum and incremental delivery.
Inform the Product Owner's functional manager.

note: Scrum Master coaches effective Scrum practice; Sprint Retrospective inspects interactions and improves effectiveness. This does not require waiting until the Retrospective to address the problem.

prompt: A Scrum Team is experiencing a growing list of impediments. Which techniques would be most helpful in this situation?

options.text: Arrange a triage meeting with management.
As a Scrum Team, prioritize the list and work on them in order.
The Scrum Master discusses the impediments with the Scrum Team.
The Product Owner should add the open impediments to the Product Backlog.

note: Scrum Master causes impediment removal while supporting self-management. Collaborative prioritization and discussion are the strongest applications here; not every impediment is product work.

prompt: Which three behaviors demonstrate that a Scrum Team is self-managing?

options.text: The Scrum Team has all the skills needed to create an Increment.
Developers collaboratively selecting their own work during the Sprint.
The Developers create their own Sprint Backlog, reflecting all work that is part of the Definition of Done.
The Scrum Team members are working within the boundaries of their functional description and nicely handing off work from analyst to developer to tester to integration.
The Scrum Master is no longer needed.
Stakeholders are attending the Daily Scrum to check progress and work with the Scrum Master to optimize the functional scope for the Sprint.

note: Likely intended answer A B C; this answer should be reviewed. Scrum Team defines internal decisions about who does what, when and how as self-management, supporting B and C. A instead defines cross-functionality; it is not by itself evidence of self-management. The other alternatives do not supply a sound third self-management behavior.

prompt: Which are appropriate topics for discussion in a Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: The value of work currently represented in the Product Backlog.
Definition of Done.
How the Scrum Team does its work.
Arranging the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
Team relations.

note: Sprint Retrospective explicitly inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools and the Definition of Done to improve quality and effectiveness.

prompt: When is the Sprint Backlog created?

options.text: During Sprint Planning.
Prior to Sprint Planning.
During refinement.
During the Sprint Retrospective.

note: Sprint Planning creates the Sprint Goal, selected Product Backlog items and delivery plan that together form the Sprint Backlog.

prompt: The Scrum Master observes the Product Owner struggling with ordering the Product Backlog. What is an appropriate action for the Scrum Master to take?

options.text: Suggest the Product Owner extend the Sprint, so he can have more time to order the Product Backlog.
Present the Product Owner with an ordered Product Backlog to use.
Offer the Product Owner help in understanding that the goal of ordering the Product Backlog is to maximize value.
Suggest that the Developers order the Product Backlog to be sure that it is a feasible ordering of work.
Encourage the Product Owner to work with the Developers to see which items technically are fastest to implement.

note: Product Owner retains accountability for ordering and maximizing value; Scrum Master helps with effective Product Backlog management rather than taking it over.

prompt: What are two effective ways for a Scrum Team to ensure security concerns are satisfied?

options.text: Postpone the work until a specialist can perform a security audit and create a list of security-related Product Backlog items.
Add security concerns to the Definition of Done.
Have the Scrum Team create Product Backlog items for each concern.
Delegate the work to the security department.
Add a Sprint to specifically resolve all security concerns.

note: Product Backlog exposes needed work; Definition of Done expresses product quality measures that Done Increments must satisfy. Security is not deferred to a separate cleanup Sprint.

prompt: A Developer takes the Scrum Master aside to express his concerns about data security issues. What should the Scrum Master do?

options.text: Tell the Product Owner to stop further development of features until the issues are fixed.
Go check with the testers.
Create a Product Backlog item for security.
Ask the Developer to share the concern with the team as soon as possible.
Add security to the Definition of Done.

note: Transparency, Adaptation and Scrum Master's coaching support making the concern visible promptly so the self-managing team can inspect it and decide appropriate action.

prompt: User documentation is part of your Definition of Done. However, there are not enough technical writers for all teams. Your Scrum Team does not have a technical writer. What should the Scrum Team do?
context: [Related to Question 119 - same documentation scenario, but a different set of answer options]

options.text: Form a separate team of technical writers that will work on an on-demand basis for the various Product Owners. Work order will be first in, first out.
Let the user documentation remain undone and accumulate until after the last development Sprint. It will then be done by any available technical writers.
The Developers on the Scrum Team should write the user documentation.
Wait until you have a technical writer on your Scrum Team to take care of this.

note: Developers create every aspect of a usable Increment and adhere to the Definition of Done. A specialist shortage does not make unfinished documentation Done.

prompt: Who owns the Sprint Backlog?
context: [Related to Question 25 - asks who owns the whole Sprint Backlog, not when an individual becomes sole owner of an item]

options.text: The Product Owner.
The Scrum Team.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.

note: Sprint Backlog describes it as a plan by and for the Developers.

prompt: When multiple Scrum Teams are working on a single product, what best describes the Definition of Done?
context: [Related to Question 14 - same multi-team Definition of Done topic, but a different set of answer options]

options.text: When multiple Scrum Teams are working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
Each Scrum Team defines and uses its own. The differences are discussed and reconciled during a hardening Sprint.
The Scrum Masters from each Scrum Team define a common Definition of Done.
Each Scrum Team uses its own, but must make their definition clear to all other teams so the differences are known.

note: Definition of Done explicitly requires teams working together on a product to mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

prompt: How is management that is external to the Scrum Team involved in the Daily Scrum?

options.text: The Product Owner represents their opinions.
The Scrum Master speaks on their behalf.
Managers are not required at the Daily Scrum.
Management gives an update at the start of each Daily Scrum.

note: Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, not a management status meeting.

prompt: Who determines when it is appropriate to update the Sprint Backlog during a Sprint?

options.text: The Scrum Team.
The Product Owner.
The Project Manager.
The Developers.

note: Sprint Backlog is the Developers' plan and is updated throughout the Sprint as learning occurs; scope changes are negotiated with the Product Owner when necessary.

prompt: Which of the following are topics for the Developers to discuss at the Daily Scrum as they inspect their progress toward the Sprint Goal?
context: [Related to Question 122 - similar Daily Scrum discussions, but a different set of answer options]

options.text: Are there any impediments blocking progress toward the Sprint Goal?
Why were you late?
Will today’s work negatively impact our ability to meet the Sprint Goal for the Sprint following this one?
What have we learned since yesterday, and how should we modify our plan to increase our ability to meet the Sprint Goal?
How many hours did I spend on the project yesterday?
What will I be working on tomorrow?
Are there any decisions that need to be made to maintain progress toward the Sprint Goal?

note: Daily Scrum focuses on the current Sprint Goal, adapting the plan, identifying impediments and making decisions. F can be relevant when connected to that goal, but is not as strong as the three explicitly goal-focused alternatives.

prompt: When Developers are having trouble delivering an Increment because they do not understand a functional requirement, what should they do?

options.text: Add a specialist to the Development Team.
Defer the work to a more appropriate Sprint.
Partially complete the functionality, and discuss the remaining work at the Sprint Review.
Collaborate with the Product Owner to determine what is possible and acceptable.

note: The Sprint and Sprint Goal support clarifying and renegotiating scope with the Product Owner as more is learned. "Development Team" in A is historical terminology, retained from the source.

prompt: Which two things are appropriate for a Scrum Master to do, if the Scrum Team does not have the tools and environment to completely finish each selected Product Backlog item?

options.text: Coach the Scrum Team to improve its skills, tools and environment over time and adjust the Definition of Done accordingly.
Refocus the current Sprint on establishing the Scrum Team's environment instead of delivering an Increment.
Encourage the Product Owner to accept partially done Increments until the situation improves.
Have the Scrum Team establish a Definition of Done that is actually possible to achieve given current circumstances.
Declare the Scrum Team not ready for Scrum.

note: Likely intended answer A D; this answer should be reviewed. Scrum Master supports improvements and impediment removal. However, The Sprint forbids decreasing quality, and Definition of Done requires applicable organizational minimum standards and usable Increments. D and "adjust" in A must not justify weakening those standards or relabeling unfinished work as Done. Address capability gaps and renegotiate scope instead.

prompt: At the seventh Sprint Review, the stakeholders are disappointed and angry. They have determined that the product or system being built will not meet their needs and will cost more than they are willing to spend. What factors likely led to this?

options.text: The Project Management Office (PMO) has not been engaged adequately.
The Product Owner has not been keeping the stakeholders aware of the progress of the project.
The stakeholders were not allowed to prioritize Product Backlog items.
The stakeholders have not been using the Sprint Reviews to inspect and evaluate progress.

note: Product Owner supports transparency and value; Sprint Review brings the team and stakeholders together to inspect outcomes and adapt. Stakeholders influence, but do not take over, Product Backlog ordering.

prompt: How much time is required after a Sprint to prepare for the next Sprint?

options.text: The break between Sprints is timeboxed to one-week for a one-month Sprint, and usually less for shorter Sprints.
Enough time for the requirements for the next Sprint to be determined and documented.
Enough time for the Developers to finish the testing from the last Sprint.
None. A new Sprint starts immediately following the end of the previous Sprint.
All of the above are allowed depending on the situation.

note: The Sprint explicitly starts a new Sprint immediately after the previous one concludes.

prompt: True or False: A Scrum Master fulfills the same role as a traditional Project Manager.

options.text: True
False

note: Scrum Master establishes Scrum and enables team effectiveness; Developers manage their own plan and the Product Owner manages product value. Scrum defines no Project Manager accountability.

prompt: What does it mean for a Scrum Team to be cross-functional?

options.text: The Scrum Team includes not only developers but also business analysts, architects, and testers.
Developers on the Scrum Team work closely with business analysts, architects, developers, and testers who are not on the team.
The Scrum Team includes cross-skilled individuals who are able to contribute to do what is necessary to deliver an Increment.
The Scrum Team is a virtual team drawing from separate teams of business analysts, architects, developers, and testers.

note: Likely intended answer C; this answer should be reviewed. Scrum Team defines cross-functionality as the team collectively having all skills necessary to create value each Sprint. C should not be read as requiring every individual to be cross-skilled or able to do every task, and A's particular job titles are not mandatory.

prompt: Which approach is best for Scrum Teams in order to produce valuable Increments?

options.text: Each Scrum Team works on an independent set of components.
Each Scrum Member works only as an independent layer of the system.
Each Developer works on the component where they feel that they can contribute.
Each Scrum Team is accountable for developing functionality from beginning to end.

note: Scrum Team is cross-functional and accountable for a valuable, useful Increment; Increment must be usable, not merely an unfinished component or layer.

prompt: How should a Scrum Team deal with non-functional requirements?

options.text: Make sure the release department understands these requirements, but it is not the Scrum Team's responsibility.
Manage them during the Integration Sprint prior to the Release Sprint.
Assign them to the lead developers on the team.
Ensure every Increment meets them.

note: Definition of Done requires the product's applicable quality measures to be met for work to count as an Increment. This refers to applicable requirements, not every possible future feature.

prompt: Who determines how work is performed during the Sprint?

options.text: Subject matter experts.
The Developers
The Scrum Master.
The Scrum Team.
Team manager.

note: Sprint Planning states that no one else tells the Developers how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

prompt: Which of the following are the Developers accountable for?

options.text: Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog.
Organizing the work required to meet the Sprint Goal.
Selecting the Product Owner.
Reporting productivity.

note: Developers are explicitly accountable for the Sprint plan and adapting it toward the Sprint Goal, within the team's self-management.

prompt: Every Scrum Team should have:

options.text: One Lead Developer and no more than 8 other members.
The competencies and skills needed to deliver an Increment in a Sprint.
At least one representative from each major department, such as, Quality Assurance, Development, and Marketing.

note: Scrum Team requires collective cross-functional capability, not specified departmental representatives or a Lead Developer hierarchy.

prompt: When is a Product Backlog item considered complete?

options.text: At the end of the Sprint.
When the item has gained product sponsor approval.
When the item passes all acceptance criteria.
When the item meets the Definition of Done.

note: Definition of Done states that an Increment is born the moment a Product Backlog item meets it. Acceptance criteria alone do not replace the Definition of Done.

prompt: Who does the work to make sure Product Backlog items conform to the Definition of Done?

options.text: The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Team.
The Quality Assurance Team.
The Developers.

note: Developers instill quality by adhering to the Definition of Done; Definition of Done explicitly requires Developers to conform to it.

prompt: When the Developers determine that they will not be able to finish the complete forecast, who has to be present when reviewing and adjusting the Sprint work selected?
context: [Related to Question 32 - same forecast-adjustment scenario, but a different set of answer options]

options.text: The Product Owner and all stakeholders.
The Scrum Master, project manager and the Developers
The Scrum Master and the Developers.
The Product Owner and the Developers.

note: Sprint Goal requires Developers to collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate Sprint Backlog scope without affecting the Sprint Goal. It does not mandate a separate formal meeting.

prompt: Which best describes the Product Backlog?

options.text: It is allowed to grow and change as more is learned about the product and its customers.
It provides just enough information to enable a Scrum Team to start the design phase of a product.
It contains all foreseeable tasks and requirements from which the Scrum Team can develop and maintain a complete project plan.
It is baselined to follow change management processes.

note: Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list, refined as learning occurs, rather than a frozen complete project plan.

prompt: Which of the following are true about the Product Owner role?

options.text: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog.
The Product Owner can be influenced by a committee.
The Product Owner role can be played by a committee or a team of people.
Multiple people can share the Product Owner role on a Scrum Team.
The Product Owner is one person.

note: 2017 source selection A, B, E is supported by the 2020 Guide: the Product Owner is one person, not a committee, and is accountable for Product Backlog management including ordering; others may influence the Product Backlog by convincing the Product Owner. "Role" is historical wording for the current Product Owner accountability.

prompt: Every Scrum Team must have a Product Owner and Scrum Master.

options.text: False. A Scrum Master is only required when asked for by the Development Team.
True. Each must be 100% dedicated to the Scrum Team.
True. Outcomes are affected by their participation and availability.
False. A Product Owner can be replaced by a business analyst in the Development Team.

note: 2017 source selection C is supported: the 2020 Guide defines a Scrum Team as one Scrum Master, one Product Owner and Developers. Scrum does not require full-time dedication. "Development Team" is 2017 terminology; the 2020 Guide refers to Developers.

prompt: What is a Development Team responsible for?
context: [Related to Question 173 - same accountability topic, but a different set of answer options and a different keyed option]

options.text: Organizing the work required to meet the Sprint Goal
Resolving internal team conflicts
Selecting the Product Owner
Reporting productivity

note: 2017 source selection is A and B. A is explicitly supported by the 2020 Developer accountabilities. B is a historical self-organization answer: the 2020 Guide does not list conflict resolution explicitly, but self-managing Scrum Teams decide internally how to work, and the Scrum Master may coach them. "Development Team" is now "Developers".

prompt: What enhances the transparency of an Increment?

options.text: Updating Sprint tasks properly in the electronic tracking tool
Keeping track of and estimating all undone work to be completed in a separate Sprint
Doing all work needed to meet the definition of "Done"
Reporting Sprint progress to the stakeholders daily

note: 2017 source selection C is supported: the Definition of Done creates transparency by providing a shared understanding of the work completed as part of the Increment. Scrum has no separate Sprint for undone work.

prompt: Who is responsible for engaging the stakeholders?
context: [Related to Question 50 - similar stakeholder topic, but a different set of answer options and a different keyed option]
instruction: choose the best answer among the listed options

options.text: The Development Team
The team manager
The project manager
The business analyst
The Product Owner

note: 2017 source selection E is the best of these options: the Product Owner represents stakeholder needs and maximizes product value. Historical caveat: under the 2020 Guide, the whole Scrum Team collaborates with stakeholders (see Question 50) and Developers may also engage them; the Product Owner is not the only person who does so.

prompt: Which output from Sprint Planning provides the Development Team with a target and overarching direction for the Sprint?

options.text: Sprint Review minutes
The Sprint Backlog
The release plan
The Sprint Goal

note: 2017 source selection D is supported: the Sprint Goal, created during Sprint Planning, is the single objective for the Sprint and gives coherence and focus. "Development Team" is now "Developers"; release plans are not a Scrum artifact.

prompt: If burndown charts are used to visualize progress, what does a trend line through a release burndown chart indicate?

options.text: When the project will be over if the Product Owner removes work that is equal in effort to any new work that is added.
The evolution of the cost spent on the project.
When the work remaining will likely be completed if nothing changes on the Product Backlog or the Development Team.
When all work will be completed so the Scrum Team can be released for other work.

note: 2017 source selection C describes the optional burndown technique. Historical/context caveat: release burndowns are not a Scrum requirement; the 2020 Guide mentions burn-downs only as optional forecasting practices that do not replace empiricism.

prompt: What are two ways that architecture and infrastructure are handled in Scrum?

options.text: They are added to the Product Backlog and addressed in early Sprints, while always requiring at least some business functionality, no matter how small.
They are built by a separate team through the creation of an architectural runway.
They are implemented along with functional development of the product.
They are discussed, determined, and documented before the actual feature development Sprints.

note: 2017 source selection is A and C. The Scrum Guide does not address architecture explicitly; these answers apply its rule that every Sprint produces a useful Increment, rather than separate architecture-only phases, Sprints or teams.

prompt: Who can abnormally terminate a Sprint?

options.text: The Development Team or its members
The Scrum Master
The Stakeholders
The Product Owner

note: 2017 source selection D is supported: only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel a Sprint, which may happen if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. "Abnormally terminate" is historical wording for cancellation.

prompt: Which two activities will a Product Owner engage in during a Sprint?

options.text: Update the Sprint burndown chart.
Run the Daily Scrum.
Answer questions from the Development Team about items in the current Sprint.
Prioritize the Development Team's work on the Sprint Backlog.
Work with the stakeholders.

note: 2017 source selection C and E is supported: the Product Owner helps the Developers understand Product Backlog items and works with stakeholders. The Sprint Backlog is by and for the Developers; the Daily Scrum is their event.

prompt: Why does a Development Team need a Sprint Goal?

options.text: A Sprint Goal ensures that all of the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint are implemented.
A Sprint Goal only gives purpose to Sprint 0.
The Development Team is more focused with a common yet specific goal.
Sprint Goals are not valuable. Everything is known from the Product Backlog.

note: 2017 source selection C is supported: the Sprint Goal creates coherence and focus, encouraging the Scrum Team to work together. Scrum has no Sprint 0, and the Sprint Goal allows flexibility in the exact work delivered.

prompt: A new developer is having continuing conflicts with existing Development Team members and creating a hostile environment. If necessary, who is responsible for removing the team member?

options.text: The Development Team is responsible, and may need help from the Scrum Master.
The Scrum Master is responsible, because he/she removes impediments.
The Product Owner is responsible, because he/she controls the return on investment (ROI).
The hiring manager is responsible, because he/she hired the developer.

note: 2017 source selection A is retained. Caveat: the Scrum Guide does not prescribe a team-member removal procedure; the answer applies self-management, with Scrum Master coaching and help. Organizational policies may also apply.

prompt: What three factors are best considered when establishing the Sprint length?
context: [Related to Question 45 - same Sprint-length topic, but a multiple-answer version with different answer options]

options.text: The risk of being disconnected from the stakeholders
Sprints must have the same length throughout an organization
The level of uncertainty over the technology to be used
The frequency at which team formation can be changed
The ability to go to market with a product release

note: 2017 source selection is A, C and E. The Guide fixes only Sprints of one month or less; it explains that overly long Sprints can increase complexity and risk, while shorter Sprints create more learning cycles. These factors are reasoned applications rather than a Guide checklist.

prompt: A Scrum Master is working with a Development Team that has members in different physical locations. The Development Team meets in a variety of meeting rooms and has much to do logistically (for example, set up conference calls) before the Daily Scrum. What action should the Scrum Master take?

options.text: Allow the Development Team to self-manage and determine for itself what to do.
Inform management and ask them to solve it.
Set up the meeting and tell the Development Team that is how it will be done.
Ask the Development Team members to alternate who is responsible for meeting setup.

note: 2017 source selection A is supported: the Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers, and self-managing teams decide how to make it work. The Scrum Master ensures it takes place and can coach, but does not dictate logistics.

prompt: Which of the following is required by Scrum?
context: [Related to Question 86 - same prompt, but a different set of answer options and a different keyed option]

options.text: Sprint Burndown Chart
Members must stand up at the Daily Scrum
Release Planning
Sprint Retrospective
All of the above

note: 2017 source selection D is supported: the Sprint Retrospective is a Scrum event. Burndown charts, standing up and release planning are optional practices, not Scrum Guide requirements.

prompt: Which two of the following are true about the Scrum Master role?

options.text: The Scrum Master assigns tasks to Development Team members when they need work.
The Scrum Master is responsible for updating the Sprint Burndown.
The Scrum Master helps those outside the team interact with the Scrum Team.
At the Sprint Review, the Scrum Master identifies what has been "done" and what has not been "done".
The Scrum Master teaches the Development Team to keep the Scrum meetings to their timebox.

note: 2017 source selection C and E is supported in current terms: the Scrum Master helps stakeholders and the organization work with the Scrum Team, and ensures that Scrum events are kept within their timeboxes. "Role" and "Scrum meetings" are historical wording for accountability and events.

prompt: The Product Owner makes sure the team selects enough from the Product Backlog for a Sprint to satisfy the stakeholders.

options.text: True
False

note: 2017 source selection False is supported: during Sprint Planning, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog in discussion with the Product Owner; stakeholder satisfaction does not set their forecast.

prompt: Who is responsible for clearly expressing Product Backlog Items?

options.text: The Scrum Master, or the Scrum Master may have the Development Team do it.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The business analyst who represents the Product Owner in the Development Team.

note: 2017 source selection B is supported: the 2020 Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items. The Product Owner may delegate this work, but remains accountable.

prompt: What is the accountability of the Product Owner during Sprint 0?

options.text: Make the complete project plan to commit date, budget and scope to the stakeholders.
Make sure enough Product Backlog items are refined to fill the first 3 Sprints.
Gathering, eliciting, and analyzing the requirements that will be inserted into the Product Backlog.
Determine the composition of the Development Teams so they have the capacity to deliver the completed forecast.
There is no such thing as Sprint 0.

note: 2017 source selection E is supported: the Scrum Guide defines no Sprint 0 or other special Sprint type. Every Sprint aims to produce a valuable, useful Increment.
